title: Pick the set
scenario:
Your studio keeps a reference library for Fernhill Tea, a tea-tin brand. The job is an autumn ad: the real tin, the current logo, and a warm autumn look.

The library list in the exhibit is our own sheet. The file names and sizes are made up for this case.
exhibit:
Fernhill Tea library (made up for this case)
  R1   tin-front-clean.jpg      Tin centred on plain white, even light. 4200 px.
  R2   tin-lifestyle.jpg        Tin on a busy kitchen counter with a plant, a cloth and cups. 3800 px.
  R3   tin-stock-wm.jpg         Tin on plain white. A stock-site watermark runs across the middle. 5000 px.
  R4   warm-window.jpg          Photo. Warm window light, terracotta palette.
  R5   warm-candle.jpg          Photo. Warm candle light, terracotta palette.
  R6   warm-bench.jpg           Photo. Warm morning light, terracotta palette, different props.
  R7   neon-night.jpg           Photo. Cool neon light, blue and pink.
  R8   watercolour-leaves.png   Painting. Watercolour, green and grey.
  R9   logo-2019.png            Old logo. Replaced by R10.
  R10  logo-2025.png            Current logo.

questions.prompt: Which three images make the best style set for the warm autumn look?

options.text: R4, R7 and R8: three different looks, so the model has a wide choice to draw from.
options.explanation: Runway says not to mix conflicting aesthetics in one request. A warm photo, a neon photo and a painting pull in three directions.

options.text: R4, R5 and R6: the same palette and the same kind of light, with different props.
options.explanation: Right. Runway's guide for its Recipes says to choose references that share a palette, lighting and mood, and to give a few, not one. We use the same rule for any tool.

options.text: R4 alone, because it is the best photo and one strong image is enough to set the style.
options.explanation: Runway says a few complementary images define a style more reliably than one.

options.text: R4 to R8, all five, so that nothing in the library is left out of the set.
options.explanation: A set is picked for one job. Five images with two clashing looks add confusion, not coverage.

questions.prompt: Which image is the best object reference for the tin?

options.text: R2, because a tin in a kitchen gives the model more context about how it is used.
options.explanation: Runway wants the subject clearly in focus and free of clutter. The plant, cloth and cups compete with the tin.

options.text: R3, because it has the most pixels, and Runway says to use the highest-quality source.
options.explanation: Resolution is one rule. Runway also says to avoid watermarks, and a watermark across the middle can be carried into the result.

options.text: R1: the tin is centred on a plain background in even light, with nothing blocking it.
options.explanation: Right. This matches Runway's advice for product references in its Recipes, which we use for any tool: centred, unobstructed, plain background, no watermark.

options.text: R1 and R2 together, so the model sees the tin clean and in use, in the same request.
options.explanation: Runway advises one subject per reference and a clear focus. R2 brings clutter into the request.

questions.prompt: The old logo R9 was replaced by R10. What do you do?

options.text: Mark R9 retired, note that R10 replaced it, move it to the archive, and keep only R10 in sets.
options.explanation: Right. This is the retire habit from the lesson. The archive keeps R9 for old jobs, and no set shows it.

options.text: Delete R9 for good, because old files only cause trouble and nobody will need the 2019 logo again.
options.explanation: An old job may still need R9. Retire and archive it instead of deleting it.

options.text: Put both logos in the set, so the model can see how the brand changed over the years.
options.explanation: Two logos in one set clash. The model may mix them, and the client wants the current one.

options.text: Leave both in the folder. The model will choose the newer logo by itself from the file names.
options.explanation: Nothing in the docs says a model picks the newest file. You choose the set.

questions.prompt: The art director wants a new style set for next month. How do you decide if it is better?

options.text: Use it for the whole next campaign and wait to see whether the client complains.
options.explanation: That tests the set on the client. A side-by-side test costs a few images and finds problems early.

options.text: Choose the set with the most images, because a larger set describes the look more fully.
options.explanation: More images are not better. Runway recommends a small, cohesive set, and the limits depend on the model.

options.text: Use the old set for half of each campaign and the new set for the other half.
options.explanation: That puts two looks into one campaign, which is the drift the kit is meant to stop.

options.text: Run the same three briefs on both sets, then compare the results side by side.
options.explanation: Right. This is our habit: a new set is a new version, tested on the same briefs as the old one.
